I was trying to make a pair of tongs a few days ago and I picked up a set of punches, just...not thinking. Of course I bent the ends on them on a workpiece that was well hot enough.

I since did some poking around and realized that what I need is entirely different.

I'd rather make than buy one. Is it just a matter of drawing an even taper off some heavy bar stock then filing the end flat and hardening it?

As far as construction, that's pretty much it - I vaguely recall actually seeing a video (never mind, found it) of the process a little while back. He doesn't go completely flat on the face, but that's really a matter of what you're using it for. The more important consideration for you is material choice: if you're buying, you'll want to avoid the mild steel and get something that's more shock resistant (and will harden better) like 5160 or an actual tool steel (probably H, W or S for your application).

If you bent the ends of your punch they likely got too hot. Strike once, then retract your punch, allowing it to air cool. You don't have to cool in water between every punch but don't try to hammer it in like you'd do with a nail (unless you're using a drift, i.e. a tool that resembles a punch in looks but is used to enlarge holes created by punches and chisel. example: https://youtu.be/Q72vV4_75jo?t=3m45s).
Spring steel (like 5160) is a good choice, it's cheap (used/broken car springs from scrap yard) and the higher amount of alloy elements will reduce de-hardening (although you still need to use correct technique). Some say air hardening steels are most suited for punches and slits, as tools made from this steel will regain some hardness automatically, even if you overheat them.
Personally I find slitting and drifting advantageous, especially with bigger rivets. Less material removed/punched out makes for sturdier tongs.
